passages.t: Do not be shaken: the Day has not come
passages.happening: “Now concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to Him, we ask you, brothers, not to be easily disconcerted or alarmed by any spirit or message or letter seeming to be from us, alleging that the Day of the Lord has already come” (verses 1-2).
passages.hearers:
This is the reason the letter was written. Someone had told the church that ‘the Day of the Lord has already come’, and they were badly shaken.

Paul does not know exactly how the claim reached them, so he names three ways it might have. ‘Any spirit’ means a word someone spoke in the church claiming it came from God. ‘Message’ means a spoken report or teaching. ‘Letter seeming to be from us’ means a letter that used Paul's name, or perhaps his first letter misunderstood. Some scholars think a forged letter had really arrived; others think the church had misread 1 Thessalonians.

What would ‘the Day has come’ even mean? It is not clear. Perhaps they thought their persecution was the beginning of the end. Perhaps some taught that the resurrection had already happened in some spiritual way, an idea Paul later opposed (2 Timothy 2:18). Either way, the believers were frightened.

The two words Paul uses are strong. ‘Disconcerted’ is a word used of things shaken by wind or storm; Paul says, literally, shaken ‘from your mind’. ‘Alarmed’ means to be troubled as by a sudden alarm. It is the same word Jesus used when he said, ‘do not be alarmed’ (Mark 13:7). Before he says anything about what must happen, Paul says: do not panic.

Notice how he describes the Lord's coming: ‘our being gathered together to Him’. The first letter promised that believers would be with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). That gathering has not yet happened. They have not been left out.
passages.ot:
Jesus had warned his disciples the same way: “See to it that no one deceives you” (Mark 13:5), and “When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. These things must happen, but the end is still to come” (Mark 13:7). His warning stands on the Old Testament's.

The prophets warned Israel against people who spoke falsely in God's name: “Do not be deceived by the prophets and diviners among you” (Jeremiah 29:8). And the Psalms give the steady heart Paul wants: “God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble. Therefore we will not fear” (Psalm 46:1-2).
passages.asks: Paul's first word to a frightened church is: do not be shaken. Ask what claims about the end, or about the world, have alarmed you. Ask where you heard them, and whether they match what Scripture actually says. And ask whether your hope makes you calm or anxious.

passages.t: The rebellion and the man of lawlessness, and what restrains him
passages.happening:
“Let no one deceive you in any way, for it will not come until the rebellion occurs and the man of lawlessness—the son of destruction—is revealed. He will oppose and exalt himself above every so-called god or object of worship. So he will seat himself in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God” (verses 3-4).

“Do you not remember that I told you these things while I was still with you? And you know what is now restraining him, so that he may be revealed at the proper time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work, but the one who now restrains it will continue until he is taken out of the way” (verses 5-7).

“And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of His mouth and annihilate by the majesty of His arrival” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Paul's answer is ‘not yet’. Two things must come first: ‘the rebellion’ and the revealing of ‘the man of lawlessness’.

‘Rebellion’ translates a word that could mean a political revolt or a falling away from God. Readers differ on whether Paul means a falling away within the church, a wider revolt of the world against God, or both. A few have argued that it means a ‘departure’ of believers, but most scholars do not read it that way.

The man of lawlessness is someone who sets himself against God and claims God's place. Paul's first readers knew that rulers could do this. In 167 BC a Greek king, Antiochus IV, had set up a pagan altar in the temple in Jerusalem. Only about ten years before this letter, in AD 40, the emperor Caligula had ordered his own statue set up in the temple; the order was put off, and dropped when he died. In the Greek cities, emperors were honoured with temples, priests and sacrifices. A ruler who demanded worship was not hard to picture.

Then comes the most puzzling part. Something is ‘restraining’ him, and in the next verse it is ‘the one who now restrains’, so it seems to be both a force and a person. Paul says, ‘you know what’ it is. They did. We do not.

But notice the end. The lawless one has his own ‘revealing’ and his own ‘coming’, the very words Paul uses of Jesus. He is a counterfeit. And the real Lord ends him with a breath.
passages.ot:
The figure looks like the proud kings of the prophets. Daniel saw a king who “will exalt and magnify himself above every god, and he will speak monstrous things against the God of gods” (Daniel 11:36), whose forces would “set up the abomination of desolation” in the temple (Daniel 11:31). Isaiah mocked the king of Babylon, who said, “I will make myself like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14). Ezekiel told the ruler of Tyre, “Yet you are a man and not a god” (Ezekiel 28:2).

And the lawless one's end comes from Isaiah's promised king, the Spirit-filled son of David, who will “slay the wicked with the breath of His lips” (Isaiah 11:4). Paul gives that work to the Lord Jesus.
passages.hard:
Who is the man of lawlessness, and who or what restrains him?

The honest answer begins with Paul's own words: ‘you know what is now restraining him’. The Thessalonians knew, because Paul had told them in person. We are hearing one side of a conversation. Augustine, one of the greatest teachers of the early church, admitted that he did not know what Paul meant.

Christians have read the passage in several main ways, and faithful people hold each. Many, from Irenaeus in the second century to many readers today, take the man of lawlessness to be a single person who will appear shortly before Christ returns, the figure later called the Antichrist; some of them expect a temple to be rebuilt in Jerusalem. Others read the passage against Paul's own century, pointing to the memory of Caligula's statue, to the emperor Nero, or to the war that ended with the temple's destruction in AD 70. Many of the Protestant Reformers read it as speaking of the papacy of their day, a reading written into some confessions of that time; few hold it now, and Catholic Christians have rejected it. Others see a power of rebellion against God that takes shape again and again in rulers and systems through history, and will come to a head at the end.

On the restrainer, the main suggestions are the Roman Empire and its rule of law, a view found as early as Tertullian; the Holy Spirit, or the Spirit at work through the church, a view common among those who expect a rapture before the time of trouble; the preaching of the gospel to the nations; the archangel Michael; or God himself.

No reading is certain. Each can point to something in the text, and none has settled the question. These notes do not choose. They identify the man of lawlessness, and the one who restrains him, with no living person, church, pope, nation, leader or movement. In many centuries people have named someone of their own day and expected the end at once. The end did not come, and such claims have often frightened believers and turned Christians against one another. The site's chapter note on 2 Thessalonians 2 and the study on the end times set out the readings more fully.

Paul wrote this passage to steady frightened people, not to feed speculation. Whatever the details, three things are plain. The Day had not come. Evil is real, but it is held in check. And it will end with one breath from the Lord Jesus.
passages.asks: Paul tells the church that evil is held back and will be ended by the Lord Jesus. Ask whether you are more fascinated by the identity of the lawless one than by the Lord who defeats him. Ask where you see people, including yourself, grasping at God's place. And ask whether you trust that nothing in history is out of God's hands.

passages.t: False wonders, and those who refuse the truth
passages.happening:
“The coming of the lawless one will be accompanied by the working of Satan, with every kind of power, sign, and false wonder, and with every wicked deception directed against those who are perishing, because they refused the love of the truth that would have saved them” (verses 9-10).

“For this reason God will send them a powerful delusion so that they believe the lie, in order that judgment may come upon all who have disbelieved the truth and delighted in wickedness” (verses 11-12).
passages.hearers:
The lawless one will come with ‘power, sign, and false wonder’. Those are the same words the New Testament uses for real miracles. So a miracle alone does not prove that something is true. A wonder can serve a lie.

Who is deceived? Paul says it is those ‘who refused the love of the truth’. Notice the words. It is not that they never heard the truth, or that they had honest questions. They refused to love it. They ‘delighted in wickedness’. The deception works on hearts that have already turned away.

Then comes the hardest line: ‘God will send them a powerful delusion’. Paul is not saying that God tricks honest people. He is saying that God, in judgment, gives people over to the lie they have chosen. They wanted it, and he lets them have it. Paul says the same in Romans: when people would not honour God, ‘God gave them over’ to what they desired (Romans 1:24).

The Thessalonians were not in this group. The next verses say so plainly.
passages.ot:
The law warned that a false prophet might work a real sign, and still must not be followed: “you must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer. For the LORD your God is testing you to find out whether you love Him with all your heart” (Deuteronomy 13:3).

God giving people over to what they chose is a sad thread in the Old Testament. “But My people would not listen to Me, and Israel would not obey Me. So I gave them up to their stubborn hearts to follow their own devices” (Psalm 81:11-12). “So they will eat the fruit of their own way, and be filled with their own devices” (Proverbs 1:31).

And once God allowed a lying spirit to mislead a king who wanted only flattering prophets (1 Kings 22:22-23).
passages.hard:
‘God will send them a powerful delusion.’ Does God deceive people?

Paul is describing judgment, not trickery of the innocent. Those who are deluded are those who ‘refused the love of the truth’ and ‘delighted in wickedness’. God gives them what they have chosen. That is a pattern the Bible shows more than once: God hands people over to the path they insist on.

This passage is not about people who are honestly searching, or who struggle with doubt. If you are worried that you have been given over to a lie, the worry itself shows a heart that still cares for the truth. Those whom Paul describes do not love the truth at all. The way to Christ is still open, and the next verses speak of God choosing and calling people through the gospel.
passages.asks: Paul says deception works on people who refuse to love the truth. Ask whether you love the truth even when it is uncomfortable, or only when it agrees with you. Ask what wonders or claims you are tempted to believe because you want them to be true. And ask whether there is any wickedness you have started to enjoy.

passages.t: Chosen and called: stand firm and hold on
passages.happening:
“But we should always thank God for you, brothers who are loved by the Lord, because God has chosen you from the beginning to be saved by the sanctification of the Spirit and by faith in the truth. To this He called you through our gospel, so that you may share in the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ” (verses 13-14).

“Therefore, brothers, stand firm and cling to the traditions we taught you, whether by speech or by letter” (verse 15).

“Now may our Lord Jesus Christ Himself and God our Father, who by grace has loved us and given us eternal comfort and good hope, encourage your hearts and strengthen you in every good word and deed” (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
‘But’ turns everything around. After those who refuse the truth come those whom God has chosen. Against the lie, the truth. Against delusion, faith. Against judgment, glory.

Notice how much is God's doing. He loved them. He chose them. The Spirit makes them holy. He called them through the gospel. And the goal is that they ‘share in the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ’. Their part is ‘faith in the truth’.

There is a small difference among the Greek copies in verse 13. Some read ‘from the beginning’, as the BSB does. Others read ‘as firstfruits’, the first part of a harvest given to God. The two differ by one letter in Greek. Paul calls early converts ‘firstfruits’ elsewhere, which supports one reading; ‘from the beginning’ stresses God's eternal choice, which supports the other.

Then: ‘stand firm and cling to the traditions’. A tradition is something handed on. Here it means what the apostles taught them, in person and in writing. Christians read this verse differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians see in it the church's handed-down teaching held together with Scripture. Protestant Christians read the apostles' traditions as now found in Scripture, which tests all later teaching. These notes do not choose. All agree that the church must hold on to what the apostles taught.

And the prayer at the end names Jesus first, before the Father, as the giver of ‘eternal comfort and good hope’. A frightened church needs comfort, and here it is.
passages.ot:
God's choosing of his people rests on love. “For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The LORD your God has chosen you” (Deuteronomy 7:6). “I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have drawn you with loving devotion” (Jeremiah 31:3).

Holding on to what was handed down is the law's own command: “And you shall teach them diligently to your children” (Deuteronomy 6:7). Jeremiah told the people, “Ask for the ancient paths: ‘Where is the good way?’ Then walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls” (Jeremiah 6:16).

And God is the one who comforts: “Comfort, comfort My people,” says your God (Isaiah 40:1).
passages.asks: After the hard words about delusion, Paul reminds the church that God loved them, chose them and called them. Ask whether you believe that about yourself. Ask what you have been taught that you need to hold on to more firmly. And ask where you need God's comfort and good hope today.
